conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the internal medicine doctors looking after you. You were just brought up from the procedure suite after your bronchoscopy and balloon dilation. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey doc. Throat hurts... kind of sore around the trach. But I’m okay, I guess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You had a procedure today to open up some narrowing in your airway, so some soreness is expected. We’ll manage your pain carefully. Any trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, breathing’s about the same. Still wheezing a bit, but that’s normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lungs have been doing that for a while. The team said the procedure went smoothly—no complications. You’ll stay with us for a few days to control the pain and make sure everything stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve done this before. Just want to get back home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work toward that. For now, you’ll get acetaminophen every 8 hours and ibuprofen every 6 hours as needed. Oxycodone is available for breakthrough pain—just let the nurse know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like taking too much of that oxycodone. Makes me foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll use it only when needed and taper it as your pain improves. Most patients stop it within a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And I need my oxygen at night, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on your usual home oxygen regimen through the trach. We’re monitoring your oxygen levels, and they’re good—96% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I just reviewed your labs. Your white blood cell count is a bit high—18.0—probably from the procedure or mild inflammation. Nothing suggests infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. It’s common after procedures like this. We’ll watch it, and it should come down in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, can I sit up more? I feel okay, just a little sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re stable. We encourage moving around as tolerated. Just call for help if you feel dizzy or short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain still the main issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, throat’s still sore. Took ibuprofen last night, helped a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that up. Your breathing sounds are still wheezy, but no new concerns. We’re continuing your prednisone as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pirfenidone? I haven’t been taking it—ran out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not available here due to formulary rules, but the interventional pulmonology team will help you get it set up as an outpatient. It’s not urgent to restart right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I just didn’t want it forgotten.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it’s coordinated before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs are back. White count dropped to 9.4—much better. Hemoglobin is stable. This is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Your body is recovering as expected. Pain should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How’s the pain today—better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, much better. Didn’t need any oxycodone last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll stop the oxycodone and keep you on acetaminophen and ibuprofen as needed. You’re right on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow or the day after. We want to make sure your pain is well-controlled without opioids and that you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy—what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. The tissue from your airway showed squamous metaplasia and mild chronic inflammation. No infection or cancer. It’s consistent with your long-term airway changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing urgent or dangerous. It explains the narrowing and why you need these procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Vital signs are excellent—heart rate 81, blood pressure 133/80, oxygen 98% on trach mask. Lungs sound much clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll confirm the plan with your pulmonologist, and the team will help set up your follow-up and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another dilation soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s up to your pulmonologist, but these are usually scheduled every few months based on symptoms. You’ll have a follow-up appointment to discuss that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge order is in. You’ll go home tomorrow morning if all stays well tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my trach? It feels okay, but I want to make sure I’m taking care of it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The nurse will review trach care with you—cleaning, suctioning, and signs of infection or blockage. You’ve done this before, but a refresher helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it starts hurting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the acetaminophen and ibuprofen as prescribed. If pain worsens or you develop fever or breathing trouble, call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially ready for discharge. We’ve arranged your follow-up with pulmonology and helped start the process for your pirfenidone prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Continue the home meds, including prednisone as directed. Watch for any breathing changes or signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep using oxygen at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. The nurse will go over your discharge papers and answer any last questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Everyone’s been great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care, and see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say thanks again before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check-in—still feeling good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no pain, breathing fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Discharge is confirmed for this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nurse said I can leave soon. Just waiting on the ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll stop by one last time to say goodbye before you go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged. Take it easy, follow up as scheduled, and keep managing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doc. Really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe and well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just letting you know—I’m about to head out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Have a smooth recovery at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. See you in clinic.
